theory.intro: Area is measured in square units. Choosing a unit means picking the square that best matches the surface being covered, so the measurement comes out as a number that is easy to read and easy to picture.
facts: $\text{mm}^2$ (square millimetres) suit tiny surfaces: an ant's head, a watch battery, the eye of a needle.
$\text{cm}^2$ (square centimetres) suit small flat objects: a stamp, a phone screen, a page.
$\text{m}^2$ (square metres) suit rooms and floors: a desk top, a carpet, a classroom.
**Hectares (ha)** suit land: a paddock, a park, a sports ground. $1\text{ ha}$ is the area of a square $100$ m by $100$ m.
$\text{km}^2$ (square kilometres) suit very large regions: a suburb, a national park, a country.
The best unit gives a number that is neither enormous nor much smaller than $1$. A bedroom reads better as $12\text{ m}^2$ than as $120\,000\text{ cm}^2$.
steps: Picture how big the surface is.
Compare it with a benchmark: a fingernail, a page, a room, a paddock, a suburb.
Choose the unit that gives a number that is easy to say and write.

foundation.question_text: Which unit of area is most appropriate for the head of an ant: $\text{mm}^2$, $\text{cm}^2$, $\text{m}^2$, ha or $\text{km}^2$?
foundation.solution_text:
An ant's head is only about a millimetre across.
A square millimetre is the square that matches a surface that small.
$\text{mm}^2$

foundation.question_text: Which unit of area is most appropriate for a page of an exercise book: $\text{mm}^2$, $\text{cm}^2$, $\text{m}^2$, ha or $\text{km}^2$?
foundation.solution_text:
A page is roughly $20$ cm across and $30$ cm down.
A square centimetre fits onto a page a few hundred times, which is a sensible count.
$\text{cm}^2$

foundation.question_text: Which unit of area is most appropriate for the floor of a classroom: $\text{mm}^2$, $\text{cm}^2$, $\text{m}^2$, ha or $\text{km}^2$?
foundation.solution_text:
A classroom is several metres across in each direction.
A square metre is the square that matches a room-sized floor.
$\text{m}^2$

foundation.question_text: Which unit of area is most appropriate for a farmer's paddock: $\text{mm}^2$, $\text{cm}^2$, $\text{m}^2$, ha or $\text{km}^2$?
foundation.solution_text:
A paddock is hundreds of metres across, far bigger than a room but far smaller than a suburb.
Hectares are the unit used for land of that size.
ha

foundation.question_text: Which unit of area is most appropriate for the island of Tasmania: $\text{mm}^2$, $\text{cm}^2$, $\text{m}^2$, ha or $\text{km}^2$?
foundation.solution_text:
Tasmania stretches hundreds of kilometres in each direction.
Only the square kilometre is large enough to give a manageable number.
$\text{km}^2$

foundation.question_text: Which of $\text{mm}^2$, $\text{cm}^2$ and $\text{m}^2$ is the largest unit of area?
foundation.solution_text:
A metre is longer than a centimetre, which is longer than a millimetre.
The square built on the longest side covers the most space.
$\text{m}^2$

foundation.question_text: Which is the larger unit of area, $1$ ha or $1\text{ km}^2$?
foundation.solution_text:
A hectare is the square with sides $100$ m; a square kilometre is the square with sides $1000$ m.
The square kilometre is built on the longer side, so it covers more ground.
$1\text{ km}^2$

foundation.question_text: A region has an area of about $3$ ha. Is it more likely to be a bedroom floor or a school oval?
foundation.solution_text:
Hectares are used for land, and a bedroom floor is only a few metres across.
A school oval is the only one of the two big enough to be measured in hectares.
A school oval.

development.question_text: A tennis court has an area of about $260$ square metres. Would you record this area in $\text{m}^2$ or in ha? Give a reason.
development.solution_text:
In hectares a tennis court is only a small fraction of a hectare, so the number would sit well below $1$.
In square metres it is $260$, a number that is easy to read and compare.
$\text{m}^2$

development.question_text: Would you record the size of a whole suburb in ha or in $\text{km}^2$? Give a reason.
development.solution_text:
A suburb is several kilometres across, so in hectares it would run into the thousands.
Square kilometres keep the number small enough to read at a glance.
$\text{km}^2$

development.question_text: Jai records the area of a postage stamp as $0.0005\text{ m}^2$. His measurement is correct. Explain why $\text{m}^2$ is not the most appropriate unit here, and state a better one.
development.solution_text:
A square metre is far bigger than a stamp, so the measurement comes out as a decimal much smaller than $1$ and is hard to picture.
A stamp is a few centimetres each way, so the square centimetre matches it.
$\text{cm}^2$

development.question_text: Mia measures her bedroom floor and writes the area as $120\,000\text{ cm}^2$. Explain why $\text{cm}^2$ is not the most appropriate unit here, and state a better one.
development.solution_text:
A square centimetre is far smaller than a bedroom, so the count runs to six digits and is hard to compare with other rooms.
A bedroom is a few metres each way, so the square metre matches it.
$\text{m}^2$

development.question_text: A real-estate advertisement gives a house block as $0.00065\text{ km}^2$. Explain why this unit is a poor choice, and give a better one.
development.solution_text:
A square kilometre covers a whole neighbourhood, so a single block comes out as a decimal with three leading zeros.
A house block is tens of metres each way, so the square metre gives a whole number a buyer can picture.
$\text{m}^2$

development.question_text: Which of these is most likely to have an area of about $1\text{ m}^2$: a postage stamp, a beach towel or a tennis court?
development.solution_text:
A square metre is about the size of a small table top.
A stamp is far smaller and a tennis court is far larger.
A beach towel.

development.question_text: A surface has an area of about $150\text{ mm}^2$. Which is it most likely to be: a fingernail, a dinner plate or a doormat?
development.solution_text:
$150\text{ mm}^2$ is the area of a square roughly $12$ mm by $12$ mm.
A dinner plate and a doormat are both far wider than that.
A fingernail.

development.question_text: Put these units of area in order from smallest to largest: ha, $\text{cm}^2$, $\text{km}^2$, $\text{mm}^2$, $\text{m}^2$.
development.solution_text:
The squares are built on sides of $1$ mm, $1$ cm, $1$ m, $100$ m and $1000$ m.
Ordering the sides orders the squares.
$\text{mm}^2$, $\text{cm}^2$, $\text{m}^2$, ha, $\text{km}^2$

mastery.question_text: A science display labels the area of four things: a fingernail, a bath towel, a wheat paddock and the Australian Capital Territory. Choose the most appropriate unit for each, and state the rule you used to decide.
mastery.solution_text:
A fingernail is about a centimetre each way, so a square centimetre would give a number near $1$ and a square millimetre gives a readable count: $\text{mm}^2$.
A bath towel is more than a metre long: $\text{m}^2$.
A wheat paddock is hundreds of metres each way: ha.
The Australian Capital Territory is tens of kilometres each way: $\text{km}^2$.
The rule is to pick the unit whose square is closest in size to the surface, so the measurement is neither a huge count nor a decimal well below $1$.

mastery.question_text: A museum's record sheet has one area column and the curator wants a single unit used for every exhibit, from a coin to a courtyard. Explain the two problems this creates, and name the unit you would use for each of those two exhibits if the rule were dropped.
mastery.solution_text:
If the shared unit is small, such as $\text{mm}^2$, the courtyard's area becomes a number with seven or eight digits that nobody can picture.
If the shared unit is large, such as $\text{m}^2$, the coin's area becomes a decimal with several leading zeros and rounds away to nothing.
No single unit sits close to both sizes, so one entry is always unreadable.
A coin suits $\text{cm}^2$ and a courtyard suits $\text{m}^2$.

mastery.question_text: A school's grounds can be written as $25\,000\text{ m}^2$, $2.5$ ha or $0.025\text{ km}^2$, and all three are correct. Which would a real-estate advertisement use, and why?
mastery.solution_text:
$0.025\text{ km}^2$ is a decimal well below $1$, so the size is hard to picture.
$25\,000\text{ m}^2$ is a five-digit count, which is accurate but clumsy to compare with other listings.
$2.5$ ha is a short number close to $1$, and hectares are the unit buyers already use for land.
$2.5$ ha
